Q: Grouping text rows in equal-sized groups A:

An interesting task. I will propose such a solution. Finding a compromise between the length of the group name and the stability of the group size.
To shorten the name of the group, you need to identify neighboring words that differ in their initial characters.

least(
          case when substring(ItemName,1,1)<>substring(nextItem,1,1) then  1 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,2,1)<>substring(nextItem,2,1) then  2 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,3,1)<>substring(nextItem,3,1) then  3 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,4,1)<>substring(nextItem,4,1) then  4 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,5,1)<>substring(nextItem,5,1) then  5 end
          ) nextDif

For example pair (AABOP, AAGNX) ->nextDiff=3 and for (AOJ7S , BCEUV)->1. Less value of "nexdDif" is preferable for group bound (start of group).
Less prevDif is start of group and less nextDif is end of group.

I use "prevDiff" as a weighting component when selecting the start of the group. For first word "prevdif" is manually set to min value (0).

Next, we denote the rows that may be the beginning of a new group. The beginning of a new group should be based on the "groupSize"*N of the rows +- tolerance("tlr"). I took the tolerance as sqrt(sqrt(ItemCount)). This is quite arbitrary, but it should be consistent with practice.
For example, if groupSize=17 and tlr=2 , we consider start of 2-nd group in rows 15,16,17,18,19.

As a result, the
"prevDiff" - difference of two rows and "grShift" -the distance of the current row from the "calculated" beginning of the group
are involved in weighing the position.

Next, we choice row with less weight in selected rows (15,16,17,18,19).
I use weight formula

prevDif*0.25 + 0.75 * power(sin(pi() * grShift / groupSize),2) as score

After weighing, we save only the rows - the beginning of the group. This makes it easier to add new rows, since the group occupies the range from the beginning word to the beginning word of the next group, without including it.

with word_dif as(
  select *
      ,round((rn+tlr)/groupSize) bn
  from(
    select *
      ,lead(prevDif,1,0)over(partition by ItemType order by ItemName)nextDif
      ,abs(rn- (floor(rn/groupSize+0.5)*groupSize)) grShift
      ,floor(sqrt(groupSize)/2) tlr
    from(
      select *
        ,least(
          case when prevItem is null then  0 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,1,1)<>substring(prevItem,1,1) then  1 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,2,1)<>substring(prevItem,2,1) then  2 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,3,1)<>substring(prevItem,3,1) then  3 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,4,1)<>substring(prevItem,4,1) then  4 end
         ,case when substring(ItemName,5,1)<>substring(prevItem,5,1) then  5 end
          ) prevDif
        -- ,ceiling(sqrt(itemCnt)) groupSize
        ,sqrt(itemCnt) groupSize
      from(
        select ItemType,upper(ItemName) ItemName 
          ,lag(upper(ItemName),1,'')over(partition by ItemType order by ItemName) prevItem
          ,lead(upper(ItemName),1,'zzzzzzz')over(partition by ItemType order by ItemName) nextItem
          ,row_number()over(partition by ItemType order by ItemName) rn
          ,count(*)over(partition by ItemType) itemCnt
        from test
      ) a
    )b
  )c
)
,weighted as(
  select *
    ,row_number()over(partition by ItemType,bn order by score ) minScoreRn
  from(
    select * 
      ,prevDif*0.25 + 0.75 * power(sin(pi() * grShift / groupSize),2) score
    from word_dif
    where grShift<=(tlr+4)  -- try change tolerance value
  )c
)
, group_heads as(
select case when minScoreRn=1 then 'b' else '' end grHead
  ,sum(case when minScoreRn=1 then 1 else 0 end)over(partition by ItemType order by rn) grn
  ,ItemType,ItemName,prevItem,rn,prevDif,nextDif, grshift,bn, score, minscorern
  ,tlr,groupSize,nextItem,itemCnt
from weighted
-- where minScoreRn=1
)
select left(ItemName,prevDif) fromWord
  ,lead(rn,1,itemCnt)over(partition by ItemType order by rn)-rn+1 grsizeFact
  ,*
from group_heads
where minScoreRn=1
order by rn;

Q: I want to take (B → (C → B)), and turn it into (¬(C) → (B → ¬(C))) using the mapping {B=¬(C), C=B} A:

If the map keys will be individual characters exclusively, you could literally map the characters in the input string.

def map_symbols(symbol_map: dict[str, str], input_character: str) -> str:
    return symbol_map.get(input_character) if input_character in symbol_map else input_character

def sub_formula(symbol_map: dict[str, str], formula_string: str) -> str:
    return "".join(map(lambda character: map_symbols(symbol_map, character), formula_string))

The above prints (¬(C) → (B → ¬(C))) when the example formula and mapping are passed as arguments.

Q: How can I avoid using LLMs as a software developer? A:

It is thinking instead of me

Make your own analysis and describe how you would implement the solution, so that it does exactly what you tell it to and nothing more, then review the output as if an intern submitted a merge request, see how if differs from what you envisioned, and fix it.

In this way, its only purpose would be helping you output approximately what you would have done, but maybe faster depending on your top typing speed.

Q: What is copy-on-write (COW) memory? A:

Here I will explain a few things: What copy-on-write (COW) is and how it consumes the memory, why setting 'vm.overcommit_memory = 1' won't help the memory usage and performance issue, and best practices of backing up Redis data.

Copy-on-write and its memory usage

Redis' snapshot backup leverage the COW semantics, which is provided by modern operating system to resolve the issue that when forking processes, the memory of the parent process is copied to the child process thus doubles the memory footprint. In COW, the forked child process will share the original memory space of the parent process. It only copies the memory page when either process modifies that memory page. Here is an illustration of the memory space before data modification and after data modification:

When the Redis' RDB backup is ongoing, there will be data changes happening in the parent process, which is accepting new requests from clients and handling it in the memory. If the query rate (unit QPS) is high, the parent process will copy tons of memory pages for the new changes during the child process' backup time. Thus the parent process will consume extra memory. In extreme cases, if all of the memory pages are modified, the memory footprint of the Redis instance will be doubled. Yeah, there is a possibility that the memory is doubled, and this fact will explain why Redis provides the "overcommit_memory=1" option, and what problem it can resolve, what it cannot (reducing the memory usage).

What "vm.overcommit_memory = 1" is, and what issues it resolves

During the RDB backup, you may see such a log error:

10202:M 13 Sep 11:34:16.535 # Can't save in background: fork: Cannot allocate memory

It indicates there is not enough memory to fork the child process to do the backup. If the Redis process consumes 2 GB memory now, when forking the child process, operating system will assume you have another 2 GB memory, so that in extreme cases of COW, there is sufficient memory to copy all dirty memory pages. Even the extra memory is not used yet when forking the child process, it checks the idle memory to avoid later out-of-memory errors. In the Redis log, it provides the solution:

10202:M 13 Sep 11:33:09.943 # WARNING overcommit_memory is set to 0! Background
save may fail under low memory condition. To fix this issue, add
'vm.overcommit_memory = 1' to /etc/sysctl.conf and then reboot or run the
command 'sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1' for this to take effect.

So setting 'vm.overcommit_memory = 1' will allow you to fork the child process when the idle memory is low. If you know the dirty memory pages during the backup process won't be too many, there won't be any actual problems because the memory will be allocated successfully every time a new COW operation happens.

And, 'vm.overcommit_memory = 1' only guarantees that you can fork the child process to backup the Redis data, but it cannot reduce the memory usage if there are writing operations happening all the time in the parent process.

Redis backup practice

There are three ways of persisting the Redis memory data: RDB (snapshotting), AOF, and the hybrid of the two. Any approach will impact the server response time to some extent, no matter how you configure the settings. To minimize the impact of the persisting process, we normally run the backup in slave instance instead on the master instance. However, there is a new risk if we do it on a slave. When there is network partitions happening, the slave may not be able to keep up-to-date, so backing up on a slave will risk losing some data.

One resolution is to have multiple slaves, so the chance of having all of them out-of-sync with the master instance is lowered. Another prevention is setting up robust monitoring system, so we can detect network issues sooner and reduce the time span of the network partition.
